_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Mathematics unit lecture film, Lesson 4 Parts of a Whole. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in the beat that names it. The chapters follow the lesson page's own teaching steps in order - step 4 More parts, smaller parts; step 5 A fraction is a division (3 cakes between 4 children); step 6 A fraction of an amount (one fifth of 20); step 8 Same value, different name; step 9 Out of a hundred (25 of 100); step 10 Which is bigger (three quarters against five eighths) - with the lesson's own numbers. Every division drawn here is equal by construction: ART.fraction cuts its bar into parts of exactly bw/parts, and the equivalence bars are the same drawing placed at the same width, so 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 shade the same length.
title: Parts of a Whole
subtitle: Grade 4 Mathematics
objectives: Understand that the more parts a whole is divided into, the smaller the parts become.
Understand that a fraction can be represented as a division of the numerator by the denominator (unit fractions and three-quarters).
Understand that unit fractions can act as operators.
Recognise that two proper fractions can have an equivalent value.
Understand percentage as the number of parts in each hundred, and use the percentage symbol (%).
Use knowledge of equivalence to compare and order proper fractions, using the symbols =, > and <.

beats.say: Cut a whole into equal parts, and every part is a fraction.
Today you compare fractions, share amounts, and write percentages.
Here is one whole bar. Cut it into 2 equal parts.
Each part is a half. Now cut the same bar into 4 equal parts.
Each part is a quarter, and a quarter is half the size of a half.

at.halfsize: half the size of a half

beats.say: Cut the bar into 8, and each part is an eighth. Smaller again.
The whole never changes, so more parts always means smaller parts.
So a bigger bottom number does not mean a bigger piece.
Three cakes are shared fairly between four children.
Cut every cake into quarters. That gives twelve equal quarters.
Now share the twelve quarters out, one at a time.
Each child gets three quarters of a cake.
Three cakes divided by four children: the cakes go on top.
A unit fraction is an instruction. Find one fifth of 20.
The bottom number says how many equal groups to make, so make five.
Share the 20 counters out fairly. Each group holds four.
One group is the answer, so one fifth of 20 is 4.
It is not 5. The 5 told you how many groups, not the answer.
Two fractions can look different and still be worth exactly the same.
Here is one half of a bar, and here are two quarters of the same bar.
The shading ends in the same place, so one half equals two quarters.
Four eighths reaches there too. All three are equivalent fractions.
Per cent means out of a hundred. Here are a hundred small squares.
Shade 25 of them, and you have shaded 25 per cent of the grid.
You write it with the per cent sign, like this: 25%.
Those 25 shaded squares fill one quarter of the whole grid.
So one quarter and 25 per cent are the very same amount.
Which is bigger, three quarters or five eighths?
Give them the same bottom number first. Cut every quarter in two.
Three quarters is the same amount as six eighths.
Now only the top numbers matter, and six beats five.
So three quarters is bigger than five eighths.
More parts means smaller parts, and a fraction is a division.
To find a fraction of an amount, share it into equal groups.
Fractions can be worth the same, and per cent means out of a hundred.
Give two fractions the same bottom number, and you can compare them.
